Guidance Lead
Uses independent tracking and dynamics to decide whether an apparent trajectory change is physical or a measurement artifact.
How does Reyes tell a real trajectory change from a measurement artefact?
By seeing whether independent sources moved, or only one
By re-running the same navigation solution with much tighter tolerances
By waiting for the next scheduled navigation update
By comparing the result against the pre-launch plan
Power Systems Lead
Reads voltage, current, power, and heat as one energy system rather than isolated meters.
Why does Shah read voltage, current and heat as one system?
They are three views of one energy budget
Three separate instruments together are more accurate than any one of them
Heat is the only quantity that can be measured directly in flight
The three meters share a single power supply
Thermal and Life Support Lead
Tracks heat and gas through the cabin and asks whether powered hardware is actually transporting what it should.
What does Brooks mean by asking whether hardware is transporting what it should?
Power to a fan is not proof that air is moving
Hardware telemetry becomes unreliable during a power-down and cannot be trusted
Transport rates can only be measured on the ground
The crew cannot hear whether a fan is running
Communications Lead
Turns wave physics, antenna pointing, range, and receiver measurements into a quantitative link diagnosis.
Why does Ito treat received power as only part of a link diagnosis?
Pointing, range and a transmitter fault all look the same in it
Received power is sampled too slowly to be useful during a fast fade
Power readings are quantised too coarsely at long range
Only frequency measurements are calibrated
Dynamics and Structures Lead
Connects torque, forcing frequency, natural modes, and measured motion to spacecraft behavior.
Why does Mensah care about the frequency something is shaken at, not just how hard?
A structure answers strongly only near its own natural frequency
Forcing at high frequency always does more damage than forcing at low frequency
Frequency determines how far the vibration travels through the hull
Accelerometers only respond above a threshold frequency
Mission Integration Lead
Challenges common-mode assumptions and makes the final decision only after independent evidence agrees.
What is Carter guarding against by demanding independent evidence?
Two instruments sharing a step can be wrong together
Crew reports become unreliable when the people making them are under stress
A single instrument cannot be calibrated in flight
Independent teams work faster than one large team
Trajectory Officer

Fits trajectories to whatever tracking exists, which on a bad shift is three
numbers taken hours apart. A fit that matches the data he has is easy; a fit
that predicts the next observation is the only kind he will sign.

He treats residuals as the real output. A pattern in what the model got
wrong points at an unmodelled force or a clock error, and both of those have
hidden themselves inside a good-looking fit before.
Why does Whitaker judge a trajectory fit by its residuals rather than by how closely it matches the tracking?
Structure in the errors shows a force or a clock the fit is hiding
Residuals are the only quantity the tracking stations report back to the room
A fit with small residuals always has small uncertainty
Residuals convert range measurements into velocity
Electrical Load Officer

Keeps the power budget, which during this flight means keeping a list of
everything aboard that consumes energy and what happens the hour after it is
switched off.

Her rule is that no load is switched off in isolation. A heater turned off to
save amp-hours becomes a thermal problem that costs more amp-hours to
reverse, and the ledger has to be kept across systems rather than within one.
Why does Ferreira refuse to evaluate a load in isolation?
Switching one off moves the cost somewhere else
Every load aboard draws the same current
Loads can only be measured while the fuel cells are running
A load's cost is fixed by its rating rather than by its use
Life Support Engineer

Works the three things a sealed cabin runs out of — heat, breathable gas and
water — and the ways they interfere with each other. Cooling the cabin
condenses water onto the coldest surfaces, and the coldest surfaces are
usually the electronics.

She measures in more than one place on principle. A single cabin sensor
reports the air beside itself, and a compartment with poor circulation can be
perfectly comfortable at the sensor and dangerous two metres away.
Why does Novak insist on carbon dioxide readings from several cabin locations?
With poor circulation the gas is not uniform, so a sensor reads its own corner
Sensors drift too quickly to be trusted individually
The crew cannot reach the primary sensor while the module is powered down for the test
Multiple readings are averaged to remove instrument noise
Link Analyst

Accounts for every decibel between the spacecraft transmitter and the ground
receiver. A fade is never mysterious to him; it is one term in a budget that
changed, and the work is finding which.

Range, antenna pointing, receiver bandwidth and transmitter health all reduce
the same received power, and they are told apart by what else changed at the
same moment rather than by the signal level itself.
How does Haldane separate a pointing problem from a transmitter failure?
By what changed alongside it — attitude, range and schedule leave traces
A transmitter failure always removes the carrier completely
Pointing errors change the frequency and failures do not
The received power alone identifies the cause without any other measurement
Structural Dynamics Engineer

Studies how a spacecraft responds to being pushed at particular rates. A
structure has frequencies at which a small repeated force produces a large
motion, and hardware that is perfectly strong at rest can fail there.

He never accepts a single accelerometer as a description of a mode. One
sensor sits at one point, and a point that happens to sit at a node reads
almost nothing while the panel beside it moves.
Why will Okoye not characterise a vibration mode from one accelerometer?
At a still point of that mode there is nothing to feel
Accelerometers cannot measure below one hertz
A single sensor cannot record frequency, only amplitude
One sensor is enough only if the pump speed is constant
Flight Dynamics Integrator

Sits between the back rooms and the loop, and her job is the one nobody else
has: deciding which of six correct answers the flight director hears first.

She keeps the anomaly log, because in a fast failure the expensive mistake is
not a wrong number but two rooms acting on different versions of the same
number an hour apart.
What does Lindqvist treat as the main risk during a fast-moving failure?
Two teams working from figures that disagree
A back room refusing to give an estimate at all
The crew asking questions over the loop
Telemetry arriving faster than it can be plotted
The correction between what an instrument reads and what is true, established against something known. A shared calibration is why two instruments can be wrong together.
A shared error that makes several measurements agree for the same wrong reason.
A frequency change caused by relative motion between source and observer.
The apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when the viewpoint moves. With a known baseline it gives a distance.
The rate at which energy is transferred or used.
Large oscillation produced when forcing is near a system natural frequency.
The unit that removes carbon dioxide from the cabin air. It cleans only the air that reaches it.
A compact description of position and velocity at one time.
The rotational effect of a force applied with a lever arm.
The box aboard the spacecraft that answers a radio pulse from the ground, which is what makes timing the round trip a distance measurement.
The Failure
Create a trusted state vector and a prioritized anomaly list before commanding the crew.

A crewed lunar spacecraft reports an explosion, falling electrical power, and contradictory telemetry. The player takes the flight-director console and must first determine what can still be measured reliably.

The bang was four minutes ago. Commander Hale reported it before any instrument did, which is the first thing that should worry you. Now three consoles hold numbers that contradict each other: one bus reads zero, the guidance computer has restarted with nothing loaded, and several cabin-pressure channels dropped together inside the same second. The integration lead, Evelyn Carter, is already saying that channels dropping together are one fault and not three. This shift you decide what is happening to the vehicle, get one agreed picture of it, and set how this room will work for the next five days. Hale, Ruiz and Sato can hear every word of this.
Use units, vectors, graphs, measurement uncertainty, common-mode failure as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
What failed: the spacecraft or the sensors?
Which explanation fits the digital alarms, independent physical checks, and shared electronics?
Mission Control

Nine minutes after the bang, several digital cabin-pressure channels drop together inside the same second. Before the crew spends oxygen and time hunting a leak, the panel has to be read as one system.
Three readouts are not three independent measurements when they share the same electronics.
a gauge can fail without the thing it measures changing
Mission Control receives a sudden cabin-pressure warning on several digital channels.

Three readouts are not three independent measurements when they share a reference circuit. A shift in that one voltage moves all of them at once, in the same direction, in the same second — which is what the panel shows and what a real leak does not do. The evidence that owes nothing to those electronics agrees: the mechanical gauge is plumbed straight to the cabin and is steady, and the acoustic monitor hears nothing. The reference voltage itself has shifted low, which names the fault.
Real cabin leak
Cabin gas is escaping, so independent pressure evidence should also move.
Common reference failure
A shared electrical reference biases several digital sensors in the same direction.
One bad pressure sensor
A single sensor has failed while the others remain independent and correct.
Communications corruption
The radio link is scrambling otherwise valid spacecraft data.
Escaping gas would move the mechanical gauge too, because that gauge needs no electronics at all. It is steady.
One failed sensor moves one channel. Three channels dropping in the same second is a shared cause, not a coincidence.
Corrupted telemetry would show as bad packets, and the radio link is clean. The numbers are arriving intact and saying something wrong.

Telemetry Analysis Room
Three consoles hold contradictory numbers. One bus reads zero, the guidance platform has restarted with no record of what it saw, and nothing has been written down in an order anyone can reconstruct.
A good emergency command works across uncertainty rather than assuming it away.
a number without its units and its time is not a measurement

A state estimate is only worth having if it survives being wrong, and the order is what makes that possible. Telemetry across the failure is overwritten within minutes, so it is frozen before anything is computed from it. Units, timestamps and calibration come next, because a fit across mixed clocks produces a confident answer that is wrong. Estimates then carry uncertainties rather than single values. And the commands that follow are the ones whose benefit holds across every state the data still allows.
Preserve the telemetry first. It is the only step with a deadline set by something other than the crew — the buffers overwrite whether or not anybody is ready.
Check units, timestamps and shared dependencies second. This is where a common-mode failure becomes visible instead of being fitted.
Build the estimates third, with uncertainties attached. A state without an uncertainty cannot be argued with or tested.
Command last, and only where the benefit survives the whole range of states still consistent with the data.
Freeze and preserve the pre- and post-failure telemetry.
Verify units, timestamps, calibration states, and shared dependencies.
Construct position, velocity, attitude, power, pressure, and temperature estimates with uncertainties.
Issue only commands whose benefits remain robust across the plausible states.
Spend the first ten minutes
Ten minutes to the next tracking pass. What does the flight director do first?
Spacecraft Systems Console

Four controllers, a crew flying a vehicle that is venting something, and ten minutes to the next tracking pass. Every subsystem wants the loop, and each believes its own problem is the one that kills the crew.
Attention is a scarce physical resource during a fast-moving systems failure.
two rooms acting on different versions of one number is worse than either acting alone
Ten minutes to the next tracking pass. What does the flight director do first?

Attention is a physical resource in an emergency, the same way propellant is, and the first decision is what spends it. Four controllers are already working one failure from four sets of numbers. Until there is a single record and a single command authority, every analysis that follows can be done twice and contradicted once — and the crew executes whichever version reaches them first. Organising the room is not a delay before the work. It is what makes the work count once.
Open one anomaly log and one command authority.
Reconstruct the electrical and pressure timeline.
Verify the trajectory and attitude independently.
Ask every subsystem for a complete report at once.
The electrical and pressure timeline is the first real analysis, and it is exactly what the log exists to hold. Start it second and it survives the shift change.
Independent trajectory verification decides whether the vehicle can come home. It is needed before the burn, not before the room is organised.
Six complete subsystem reports arrive after the tracking pass and consume the ten minutes that were supposed to prepare for it.
Find the Spacecraft
Produce a consistent trajectory estimate and identify which new observation most reduces uncertainty.
Tracking data are intermittent, and the onboard computer has restarted. The team must reconstruct position and velocity from range, bearing, and timed observations.

Nine hours after the bang, and the station carrying the whole solution sets in forty minutes. The guidance lead, Camila Reyes, will not sign the trajectory until she has one measurement that did not come through the same computer. Today you rebuild where the spacecraft is and how fast it is going, and buy the next observation. Fitting the measurements together is the job, and only one station is still up. Her trajectory officer, Dale Whitaker, wants a number now so the room can start planning the correction. Reyes wants the right number. They are both right, and there are forty minutes.
Use position, velocity, acceleration, coordinate systems, graphs of motion as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
Which measurement constrains what?
Match each quantity the state estimate needs to the measurement that provides it.
Deep-Space Tracking Station

The onboard computer has restarted and the tracking is intermittent, so the state has to be rebuilt from whatever measurements can still be taken. The room has to say what each type buys before it schedules any of them.
Navigation is a reconstruction from partial projections.
describing where something is and how it is moving takes six numbers

Navigation is a reconstruction from partial projections. Each measurement type fixes a different part of the state. The six numbers come from combining them, not from any one of them. Two are worth putting numbers to. A Doppler shift is proportional to speed divided by the speed of light. A spacecraft closing at one kilometre a second shifts a 2-gigahertz carrier by about seven kilohertz. That is small, and it is measurable to a fraction of a hertz, which is what makes Doppler the instrument of choice for a rate. Differencing is the other route to a rate. Every differencing step multiplies the measurement noise, so an acceleration recovered from two rounds of subtraction is the least certain number in the set.
Photograph the spacecraft against catalogued stars. The angle between it and stars whose places are already fixed gives the line it lies along, to the precision of the catalogue and the optics.

Compare the frequency that comes back with the frequency that was sent. Motion along the line of sight stretches or compresses the returning wave, and the fractional change in frequency equals the speed as a fraction of the speed of light.
Time a pulse out to the spacecraft and back through its transponder. Radio travels at a known speed, so half the round-trip time multiplied by that speed is the distance.
Repeat the same position measurement at recorded times. Subtracting positions gives velocity, and subtracting those velocities gives acceleration.
Direction is an angle, and the star camera is the only instrument here that measures one.
A velocity along the line of sight is carried by the returned wave itself, in its frequency.
A distance is a time multiplied by a speed, which is what the round trip provides.
Rates come from repetition — two positions give a velocity, and two velocities give an acceleration.
Direction on the sky.
Line-of-sight velocity.
Range along the line of sight.
How fast it is going, and whether that is steady.

Guidance Room

The computer restarted and lost its alignment. What is left is a range from one station, two bearing angles taken ninety minutes apart, and a Doppler trace recorded in a different time standard from either.
A useful state estimate predicts future observations and exposes its own failures.
measurements only combine when they share a frame and a clock

A state estimate is only useful if it predicts the next observation, and everything in this order exists to make that test possible. A joint fit across two time standards produces an orbit nobody can see is wrong, so the transformation comes first. The fit then has to reproduce range, angle and Doppler together rather than each in turn. What the fit got wrong is where the information is: structure in the residuals means an unmodelled force. And state and uncertainty are propagated together, because the decision is made at a later time than the data.
One coordinate system and one time standard first. Two clocks in a single fit is the error that never shows up in the residuals afterwards.
Fit range, angle and Doppler together second. Fitting them separately gives three answers and no way to choose.
Read the residuals third, for structure rather than size. Scatter is noise; a pattern is a force nobody modelled.
Propagate state and uncertainty to the decision time last. The burn happens later than the data, and the uncertainty grows on the way.
Transform all observations into one coordinate and time system.
Fit a trajectory that predicts range, angle, and Doppler together.
Examine residuals for bias or unmodeled acceleration.
Propagate the state and its uncertainty forward to the hour the burn is committed.
What holds it in the curve
Why does the spacecraft need any speed at all to stay in that orbit?
Guidance Computer Room
The free-return path swings the spacecraft round the Moon at 2,500 kilometres altitude. Somebody on the loop has asked why it does not simply fall onto the surface, and the room owes them an answer.
A curved path needs a force toward the centre, and orbital motion is that force being exactly enough.
an object moving in a circle is accelerating even at constant speed
Why does the spacecraft need any speed at all to stay in that orbit?

Circular motion is acceleration toward the centre, and here the whole of that acceleration is gravity: the spacecraft is falling the entire time, and its transverse speed turns the fall into a curve that keeps missing the surface. Get the speed wrong and the curve closes on the Moon or opens away from it. There is no outward force to balance — in the spacecraft's frame the crew feel weightless precisely because nothing is opposing gravity.
It is falling, and its sideways speed makes the fall a curve that misses.
Gravity is balanced by an outward centrifugal force, so nothing accelerates.
At that altitude the Moon's gravity is too weak to matter.
The spacecraft's own thrust holds it up against gravity.
Centrifugal force is an artefact of the rotating frame; in the inertial frame there is one force and it points inward.
Lunar gravity at that altitude is about a fifth of what it is at the surface, which is not negligible at all.
The engine is off, and it stays off for most of the return.
The Wrong Trajectory
Choose a correction that restores a safe return while preserving fuel and engine options.
The spacecraft is drifting away from its planned free-return path. The player must use Newtonian gravity and impulse to determine whether a small correction now can prevent a large correction later.

Eighteen hours in, the drift is confirmed, and this is where Whitaker and Carter stop agreeing for the rest of the mission. The path misses the entry corridor by four hundred kilometres. Whitaker wants a modest burn this shift, arguing that a correction gets cheaper the earlier it is made. Carter wants to wait for the next tracking pass, because correcting a number you have not measured properly is how a small error becomes a committed one. This shift you settle it. That is Whitaker's whole case, and this shift it is the better one. There is no more propellant coming.
Use Newton’s laws, gravity, orbits, impulse, trajectory sensitivity as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
From force to trajectory change

Orbital Analysis Room

The spacecraft is drifting off the free-return path by an amount that is small today and fatal at the atmosphere. The crew wants to know why a few seconds of thrust now beats minutes of thrust tomorrow.
Trajectory control acts on velocity now to change position much later.
a force acting on a mass produces an acceleration

The chain is Newtonian and worth stating in order, because it is the reason an early correction is cheap. An engine produces a force for a measured time. That force gives the vehicle an acceleration set by its mass, so the same engine moves a heavy spacecraft less. The acceleration changes velocity by an amount proportional to the impulse. And the new velocity changes where the vehicle is hours later — trajectory control acts on velocity now to move position much later, which is why time is the term doing the work.
Force for a measured time is where the chain starts. Everything after it is a consequence of that one product.
Force divided by mass is acceleration. The same engine on a heavier vehicle produces less of it.
Acceleration integrated over the burn is the velocity change, and it is proportional to the impulse rather than to the thrust alone.
The new velocity changes position hours later. That delay is not a weakness of the method — it is what makes a small early burn worth a large late one.
An engine produces a force for a measured time.
The force gives the spacecraft an acceleration.
Acceleration changes velocity by an impulse-dependent amount.
The new velocity changes the later orbit and encounter geometry.
Small burn, large consequence

Guidance Console
A 30,000 kg spacecraft takes 6,000 N of thrust for 20 seconds. The flight dynamics officer wants the change in speed on the loop before the burn is approved.
Orbital corrections often rely on small velocity changes applied early.
force applied over a time is an impulse
Estimate the change in speed.

Force multiplied by time is impulse, and impulse divided by mass is the change in speed. The number that comes out looks absurd next to an orbital speed measured in kilometres per second, and that is the lesson rather than a problem with the arithmetic. A few metres per second applied days from arrival moves the arrival point by hundreds of kilometres, because the vehicle carries the difference for every one of those hours. The same correction made near the atmosphere costs many times as much.
A 30,000 kg spacecraft receives 6,000 N of thrust for 20 seconds.
Estimate the change in speed.

Force times time is impulse; impulse divided by mass is the velocity change. Surface gravity has no bearing on a vehicle in free flight, and specific impulse would tell you what the burn costs in propellant rather than what it achieves.
Impulse = force × time. Velocity change = impulse ÷ mass.
What the pressure difference is for
The tank reads 40 psi and the regulator wants 15. What is the flow doing?
Life Support Lab
The oxygen tank reads 40 psi, the cabin regulator is set to 15, and the flow has fallen to half of what the plan assumed. The line is the same line it was yesterday.
Something moves through a system for one reason and is held back for another.
gas flows from higher pressure to lower pressure
The tank reads 40 psi and the regulator wants 15. What is the flow doing?

Gas moves because there is a pressure difference across the path, and how much moves depends on that difference and on how restricted the path is. Twenty-five psi of difference is still there, so a halved flow points at the path — a partly closed valve, ice at an orifice, a filter loading up — or at a reading that is not measuring what the crew think it is. Tank pressure on its own cannot promise a flow rate: the same 40 psi delivers nothing through a blocked line.
Flowing on the difference, so the fall means the difference or the path changed.
Stopped, because the regulator setting is below the tank pressure.
Set by the tank pressure alone, so 40 psi guarantees the planned flow rate through the loop.
Reversed, since the cabin is warmer than the tank.
A regulator set below tank pressure is the condition for flow, not an obstacle to it.
Tank pressure sets one end of the difference; the restriction in between sets the rate.
Temperature changes gas density and pressure a little; it does not reverse a 25 psi gradient.
Turn Without Wasting Fuel
Develop a controlled reorientation procedure that stops the rotation at the required attitude.
The main guidance platform is unavailable, and the crew must reorient the spacecraft using limited thrusters and visible reference objects.

Twenty-six hours in. The guidance platform is off to save power, one thruster quad is dead, and Hale has to turn the spacecraft ninety degrees by hand while Sato reads angles aloud. Kwame Mensah, who owns the structural dynamics, has done the sums and does not like them. This shift you agree what the rotation numbers mean, write the procedure, and work out what a thruster actually does. Every degree of turn is paid for twice, once to start it and once to stop it. Let it tumble and the antenna, the array and the burn attitude go together.
Use torque, angular acceleration, moment of inertia, angular momentum, center of mass as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
Read rotational motion
Match each situation to the most scientifically justified interpretation, control, or response. Each choice is used once.
Attitude Dynamics Lab

The main guidance platform is unavailable and the crew is about to fly the vehicle by hand. Before anybody touches a thruster the room states the rotational mechanics plainly, because each one has a consequence the crew will feel.
Attitude control is Newtonian mechanics around a center of mass.
a torque is what makes something start or stop turning

Attitude control is Newtonian mechanics about a centre of mass, and four rules cover what the crew can do. Torque is force times lever arm, so the same thruster mounted farther out turns the vehicle harder. Angular acceleration is torque divided by moment of inertia, so a vehicle that is harder to turn responds less to the same push. Equal and opposite torques for equal times leave the angular momentum where it started. And with no external torque, moving mass inside the vehicle changes its shape and its spin rate but never its total angular momentum.
Larger torque.
Smaller angular acceleration.
Approximately cancel the net angular impulse.
Total angular momentum remains conserved, though rotation distribution can change.
The same force farther from the centre of mass is a longer lever arm and therefore a larger torque. This is the term the crew can actually choose.
The same torque on a larger moment of inertia gives less angular acceleration. Harder to start, and equally hard to stop.
Equal and opposite torques for equal times cancel the net angular impulse, which is what a start pulse and a stop pulse are for.
Moving internal mass with no external torque redistributes the rotation and conserves the total. Nothing inside the vehicle can change it.
Apply the same force farther from the center of mass.
Increase moment of inertia with the same torque.
Apply equal and opposite torques for equal times.
Move internal masses while no external torque acts.

Crew Procedures Room

The guidance platform is off and the crew must turn the spacecraft ninety degrees using two thruster pairs and a window. No rate display, no attitude hold, and every pulse spends propellant the entry burn is counting on.
Rotational maneuvers require planning the braking phase before the target is reached.
nothing in space slows a rotation down on its own

Nothing damps the rotation. A torque that starts the turn keeps it turning until an equal and opposite one stops it. So starting and stopping are two decisions, and the second one has to be planned before it is needed. The crew reads attitude and rate from whatever cues still work, applies a bounded torque, coasts while watching the target come round, and brakes early enough to arrive at rest. Wait until the target arrives and you overshoot. Overshoot is paid for twice.
Attitude and rate first, from cues that do not depend on the platform that is off. You cannot aim a turn you cannot measure.
A bounded torque to begin. Bounded, because the pulse that starts the turn sets the rate that has to be cancelled later.
Coast and monitor third. This is the free part of the manoeuvre and the part where the braking point is judged.
Counter-torque last, and applied early. Braking when the target arrives is braking too late, and the overshoot costs two more pulses.
Identify current attitude and angular rate from independent cues.
Apply a bounded torque to begin rotation.
Coast while monitoring angular rate and target geometry.
Apply counter-torque early enough to stop at the target.
Torque from a thruster
Use the supplied values, show the governing relationship, and give a sensible rounded result with units and interpretation.
Guidance Console
A 200 N thruster fires at right angles, three metres from the centre of mass. The crew needs the torque before it can predict how fast the vehicle starts to turn.
Force location matters as much as force magnitude in rotational control.
a longer lever arm gives the same force more turning effect
Estimate the torque about the centre of mass.

Torque is force times lever arm times the sine of the angle between them, and at right angles that sine is one, which is why this case is the simple one. The same thruster mounted closer in would produce proportionally less turn for the same propellant. Location matters as much as magnitude, and on a vehicle this size the lever arm is the term the crew can actually choose — which pair fires, not how hard.
A 200 N thruster fires at right angles, three metres from the centre of mass.
Estimate the torque about the centre of mass.

Torque is force times lever arm times the sine of the angle between them, and at right angles that last factor is one — which is why it does not appear. The lever arm has to be measured to the centre of mass, not to whatever structure is nearest.
Torque = force × lever arm, when the force is at right angles to the arm.
The Power Budget
Build a load-shedding plan that preserves essential functions through the next critical maneuver.
Fuel cells and batteries are degraded. Every electrical load now competes with guidance, communications, thermal control, and life support.

Thirty-four hours in, and the argument changes shape. Priya Shah, who runs the power systems, has the reserve down to hours and wants everything non-essential off by the end of the shift. Aaron Brooks, on thermal and life support, says the two things on his list are the scrubber fan and the cabin heaters, and that his crew are already sleeping in everything they own. The bus is sagging at 24 volts instead of 28 while the current sits near where it should be, which is Shah's other problem. This shift you work out how long the batteries last, decide why the voltage is low, and choose what goes off.
Use current, voltage, resistance, electrical power, energy budget as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
How long can the battery last?
Use the supplied values, show the governing relationship, and give a sensible rounded result with units and interpretation.
Electrical Systems Room
The fuel cells are gone and the crew is on entry batteries days earlier than any plan allowed for. The flight surgeon wants an endurance number before the next powerdown decision.
Power is the rate of energy use; endurance depends on both energy inventory and load.
energy is a stock, and power is the rate it is drawn at
Estimate the ideal endurance.

Energy and power are different things, and the division between them is the whole calculation. An inventory in kilowatt-hours divided by a draw in kilowatts leaves hours. It is an ideal figure. It assumes the load stays flat and that every last watt-hour is available, and neither is true — a cold battery gives less than its rating. It is still the number every other decision this shift gets argued against, so it is worth having early and worth calling approximate.
The fuel cells are gone. The entry batteries hold about 18 kilowatt-hours of usable energy and the essential loads draw about 3 kilowatts.
Estimate the ideal endurance.
Energy is an inventory and power is the rate it is spent at; the hours come from dividing one by the other. Bus voltage describes how the energy is delivered and says nothing about how much there is.
Endurance = energy stored ÷ power drawn.
Why is bus voltage collapsing?
Which fault fits the voltage, current, generation, and thermal evidence?
Spacecraft Load Panel
The power bus is sagging at 24 volts instead of 28 while the total load current sits near its planned value. Engineers want to start pulling equipment off the bus.
Electrical faults are easier to localize when voltage, current, and heat are treated as parts of one energy picture.
current through a resistance drops voltage and makes heat
The spacecraft power bus sags under a normal load.

Voltage, current and heat are three views of one energy picture, and reading them together locates the fault instead of guessing at it. A resistance in the path drops voltage in proportion to the current through it, and dissipates the lost power as heat exactly where the resistance is — which is what the hot junction is. Generation is healthy, because array current is normal. Nothing new is being drawn, because the total load is near plan. What is left is the path between them.
High-resistance connection
A resistive junction drops voltage and converts electrical power to heat.
Large hidden load
An unexpected device draws much more current and pulls down the bus.
Solar-array failure
Generation falls sharply, forcing the battery to replace missing array current.
